label: 4Q246 (Aramaic Apocalypse) — Complete
summary_plain: 4Q246 is a two-column Aramaic fragment from Cave 4 at Qumran. Column 1 is largely fragmentary, depicting a vision-interpretation scene before a king. Column 2 is more complete and describes a coming ruler called 'son of the Most High' and 'son of the Creator,' whose everlasting kingdom arises when the covenant people prevail and the sword ceases from the earth. The designations in this pre-NT text predate their use in later traditions by over a century.
summary_scholarly: 4Q246 (Aramaic Apocalypse) is a two-column Aramaic manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, paleographically dated to the first century BCE. Col.1 presents a vision-interpretation scene; col.2 applies the titular designations bar elyon ('son of the Most High') and bar elah ('son of the Creator') to a coming ruler whose kingdom is described as malkuth alma ('everlasting kingdom'). The am El ('people of the Creator') arise and bring the era of conflict to a close. The text establishes that these covenant designations existed in the Qumran Aramaic tradition before they were applied in NT literature, confirming the direction of borrowing: the NT adapted pre-existing covenant language, it did not originate it.

key_terms.definition: Aramaic: 'son of the Most High' — the first titular designation given to the coming ruler in 4Q246 col.2; a covenant title predating its NT application by over a century.
Aramaic: 'son of the Creator' — the second titular designation in col.2 for the coming ruler; parallels Bar Elyon and together they form the dual covenant title of the text.
Aramaic: 'people of the Creator' — the covenant community whose arising in col.2 ends the era of conflict and brings the everlasting kingdom into force.
Aramaic: 'everlasting kingdom' — the kingdom attributed to the coming ruler in 4Q246 col.2; the same phrase appears in Daniel's Aramaic sections, confirming shared covenant vocabulary.
The official DSS designation for this fragment: Cave 4, Qumran, manuscript 246. Part of the largest single corpus of Dead Sea Scrolls discoveries (1947–1956).
Aramaic: 'judgment in truth' — how the coming ruler governs in col.2; aligns with the broader DSS covenant standard of YHWH's truth as the measure of all rule.
Aramaic/Hebrew: 'interpretation' — the visionary interpretation genre present in col.1; the scene of someone falling before a king and interpreting a vision is consistent with pesher tradition.
DSS term for a hostile foreign power (frequently Rome); may be referenced in the conflict described before the people of the Creator arise in 4Q246.
The Semitic language in which 4Q246 is composed; also used in Daniel chapters 2–7 and portions of Ezra, confirming Aramaic as a living covenant-community language alongside Hebrew.
The Qumran cave that yielded the largest number of DSS manuscripts, including 4Q246. Excavated 1952 by Roland de Vaux; material dates from approximately 300 BCE to 68 CE.

faq.question: What is 4Q246?
faq.answer: A two-column Aramaic fragment from Cave 4 at Qumran, dated paleographically to the first century BCE. Column 1 is largely fragmentary, depicting a vision-interpretation scene. Column 2 is more complete and describes a coming ruler bearing the titular designations 'son of the Most High' and 'son of the Creator,' whose everlasting kingdom arises when the covenant people prevail and the sword ceases.

faq.question: What do the designations 'son of the Most High' and 'son of the Creator' mean in 4Q246?
faq.answer: They are Aramaic covenant titles for the coming ruler described in col.2 — bar elyon (son of the Most High) and bar elah (son of the Creator). These are not divine-identity claims in the Rabbinic or Christian sense. They are covenant role designations consistent with the DSS tradition of YHWH's appointed ruler. Critically, this text predates the NT by over a century, establishing that the NT borrowed these designations from existing Aramaic covenant tradition — not the reverse.

faq.question: Who are the 'people of the Creator' in col.2?
faq.answer: The am El — the covenant community, the Hebrew people of the Yahad/Qumran tradition. Their arising ends the era of conflict: 'Until the people of the Creator arises, and everyone rests from the sword.' This is not a passive waiting but an active covenant awakening that changes the world's condition.

faq.question: What happens when the people of the Creator arise?
faq.answer: The sword ceases from the earth, all cities pay homage to the coming ruler, the Creator gives all nations into the ruler's hand, and the ruler judges the earth with truth. The resolution is total: the conflict ends, the everlasting kingdom is established, and all his ways are in truth.

faq.question: Why is 4Q246 significant for understanding the NT?
faq.answer: It establishes the direction of literary borrowing. The designations 'son of the Most High,' 'son of the Creator,' and 'everlasting kingdom' — applied to the NT's invented figure — were already present in Aramaic covenant tradition over a century before NT composition. The NT adapted pre-existing Qumran community language. Per Rule 24 of ACR's content standard: the ancient text is the source; the NT borrowed from it.

faq.question: How does the Creator act in 4Q246 col.2?
faq.answer: YHWH is active, not passive. 'The great Creator is his strength; he shall make war on his behalf, giving the nations into his hand.' The Creator intervenes militarily and covenantally on behalf of the coming ruler and his people — consistent with the DSS pattern of YHWH fighting for the Sons of Light in the War Scroll (1QM).

faq.question: What language is 4Q246 written in and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Aramaic — the spoken language of the Qumran community alongside Hebrew. The same language as Daniel chapters 2–7, portions of Ezra, and multiple other DSS texts. The presence of high-covenant designations in Aramaic confirms that bar elyon and bar elah were living terms in the community's liturgical and visionary vocabulary, not invented for the NT.

faq.question: Is 4Q246 a complete text?
faq.answer: No. Column 1 is largely fragmentary — only portions survive. Column 2 is more complete but still a fragment. The text does not give the coming ruler a personal name; the designations are titular. What survives is enough to establish the covenant vocabulary and the narrative arc (conflict → people arise → everlasting kingdom).

faq.question: What other DSS texts share vocabulary with 4Q246?
faq.answer: The Aramaic sections of Daniyel (malkuth alma — everlasting kingdom), the War Scroll 1QM (the Creator fighting for the covenant people, nations given into their hand), and the community hymns of 1QH. The 'son of' covenant-title pattern also appears in other fragments. 4Q246 is part of a coherent Aramaic covenant tradition, not an isolated curiosity.

faq.question: What is the official DSS designation '4Q246' and what does it mean?
faq.answer: 4Q = Cave 4, Qumran. 246 = the sequential manuscript number within the Cave 4 corpus. Cave 4 was excavated in 1952 by Roland de Vaux and yielded the largest single collection of DSS manuscripts. 4Q246 belongs to the official 1947–1956 excavation corpus — it carries confirmed archaeological provenance, unlike the post-2002 market fragments.
